readerTitle: Why rivals copy your product but not your edge
caseNote: 가상 비교 (생활용품 소매점 vs 포장재 제조·배송) + 실제 기업 (Toyota, GM의 NUMMI 합작) + 실제 연구 (Dierickx & Cool 1989, Barney 1991) + 가상 적용 (치과 예약 소프트웨어)
insight: 경쟁자는 눈에 보이고 돈으로 살 수 있는 것을 베낀다. 오래가는 강점은 시간이 걸려 쌓이고, 일하는 방식 속에 숨어 있고, 따라 하면 경쟁자에게 손해가 되는 것이다.
misconception: 좋은 제품이나 낮은 가격이 곧 경쟁 우위다. 경쟁자가 돈만 있으면 무엇이든 따라 할 수 있다.

sources.text: Dierickx, I. & Cool, K. (1989). Asset Stock Accumulation and Sustainability of Competitive Advantage. Management Science.
Barney, J. (1991). Firm Resources and Sustained Competitive Advantage. Journal of Management.
NUMMI (GM–Toyota joint venture, Fremont, California, from 1984): widely documented in business histories and case studies
소매점, 포장재 제조사, 치과 예약 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: NUMMI는 1984년 캘리포니아 프리몬트에서 GM과 Toyota의 합작으로 시작했습니다. GM이 NUMMI의 방식을 다른 공장으로 확산하는 데 오랫동안 어려움을 겪었다는 점은 여러 사례 연구에 나옵니다. 구체적 수치는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 연도와 표현을 다시 확인하세요.
'욕조에 물을 채우는 것처럼 쌓이는 자산'과 '시간을 돈으로 단축하기 어렵다(time compression diseconomies)'는 Dierickx & Cool(1989)의 핵심 개념입니다. 카드에는 풀어 쓴 설명만 넣었고 인용문은 쓰지 않았습니다.
Toyota가 GM 등에 공장 견학을 허용했다는 내용은 일반적으로 알려진 사실로 서술했습니다. 견학 횟수나 특정 인물의 발언은 넣지 않았습니다.
가상 사례 수치: 수납함 가격 30% 저렴, 48시간 배송, 400개 치과. 모두 설명용입니다.

cards.title: Two businesses, one good year. Only one is still ahead.
body: A home-goods store has a hit: its own storage boxes, 30% cheaper than anyone else's. A packaging maker has a different edge: it delivers custom boxes to food brands within 48 hours.
Both are winning. Within a year, rivals have copied one of them almost perfectly. The other is still ahead.

image.label: A store shelf of boxes next to a small factory loading dock
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 3D 클레이 일러스트. 왼쪽은 생활용품 매장 선반에 쌓인 수납함, 오른쪽은 작은 포장재 공장의 출고장에서 트럭에 상자를 싣는 장면. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which edge is harder to copy?
body: **The store** found an overseas factory that makes its boxes cheaply. **The packaging maker** spent years tuning machine setups, scheduling and crew training to turn orders around in 48 hours.
Which edge will rivals struggle with most?

options.text: The store's. Matching a 30% lower price is very hard
options.feedback: A low price is easy to see, and the source behind it can often be found and bought. The price looks strong, but what makes it possible is exposed.

options.text: The packaging maker's. Its speed comes from years of practice
options.feedback: A rival can see the 48 hours but not how it's done. And even knowing how, it can't skip the years of tuning. That's this lesson.

options.text: Neither. With enough money, a rival can copy anything
options.feedback: Money buys machines, products and people quickly. It buys time and habits poorly. The difference matters more than it looks.

cards.title: One rival bought the answer. The other couldn't.
body: A rival store turned a box over, read the label, and contacted the same kind of factory. Similar boxes were on its shelves in months.

A rival packaging firm bought the same machines and hired a plant manager. It still couldn't hit 48 hours. The speed wasn't in the machines. It was in hundreds of small habits: which jobs to run back to back, who fixes what, how the night shift hands over.
The store's edge was a **thing**. The maker's edge was a **way of working**.

cards.title: Barriers to imitation
body: **Barriers to imitation** are the reasons a rival can't simply copy what makes you better.

Rivals copy what they can see and buy: products, prices, features, equipment. An edge lasts when it's built over time, hidden inside how people work, or costly for the rival to copy because it clashes with the rest of its business.

image.label: An iceberg: product and price above water, habits and time below
image.brief: 빙산 인포그래픽. 수면 위에는 "Product", "Price", "Machines"(경쟁자가 볼 수 있음), 수면 아래 큰 부분에는 "Years of practice", "Team habits", "Relationships"(보이지 않음). 수면 위에 망원경을 든 작은 경쟁자 캐릭터.

cards.title: Toyota showed rivals its factories. It didn't matter much.
body: Toyota was famously open about its production methods and let other carmakers tour its plants. In 1984, GM and Toyota even opened a joint factory in California, called NUMMI.

Yet GM struggled for years to spread those methods to its own plants. What it could see, such as layouts and tools, was the easy part. The hard part lived in daily habits and trust between workers and managers.
Researchers Ingemar Dierickx and Karel Cool described why: some strengths fill up slowly, like a bathtub. Paying more doesn't fill it much faster.

cards.title: Ask what a rival would need to copy you.
body: Run your edge through these. The more "no" answers, the safer it is.

breakdown.label: Is it visible?
breakdown.detail: Products and prices are. Habits and know-how mostly aren't.

breakdown.label: Can money get it fast?
breakdown.detail: Machines, yes. Years of practice and trust, no.

breakdown.label: Would copying hurt them?
breakdown.detail: A giant chain that copies a small shop's personal service breaks its own low-cost model.

cards.softwareNote: Features are the easiest thing to copy in software. What's harder: data built up over years, integrations customers depend on, and a team that deeply knows one industry's workflow.

cards.title: Hard to copy isn't the same as worth having.
body: A strength can be unique and still not matter to customers. Check that it's something they'd pay for first.
Hidden know-how has a cost too. If it lives in three people's heads, it can walk out the door with them. Write down enough to train new people, without publishing the recipe.
And rivals don't always copy. Sometimes they go around you with a different approach that makes your edge less important.

cards.title: Now it's software for dental clinics.
body: Your booking app serves 400 dental clinics. A well-funded rival just cloned your main features and launched.
Where should your next year of effort go?

options.text: Ship new features faster than the rival can copy them
options.feedback: It keeps you ahead for a while, but features are visible and copyable. You'd be racing on the ground where the rival is strongest.

options.text: Deepen what took years: your setup playbook from 400 clinics and the team that runs it
options.feedback: The rival can see your screens, not how you get a busy clinic live in a week. That knowledge only comes from doing it hundreds of times.

options.text: Cut your price 30% to hold on to clinics
options.feedback: A price is the most visible thing of all. A funded rival can match it tomorrow, and you'd both earn less.

cards.title: Rivals copy what they can see. Build what they can't.
body: Your lasting edge is rarely the product or the price. It's what took time, lives in how your people work, or would cost a rival too much to match.
**Try it today:** write down your biggest strength. Ask: could a rival see it, buy it quickly, and afford to copy it? Count the "no" answers.
